A second easter egg, one rule about accessibility reversed and one about ancestors added, plus two rules from a settings-card report. The 2.1.0 release is folded into this one, and its tag and notes are gone with it.

**Adopting apps:** `DEFAULT_MOTION` is `subtle`, not `wild`, and if you shipped the old default, migrate any stored value that used to name the top level before you change it. Remove every `--motion-page-scale` declaration and take the `scale()` out of your own copy of `glim-page-in`; a locally re-added scale or tilt on that keyframe reproduces the defect this release removes. Nothing else moves: no level name, no attribute, no stored value.

## ✨ Added

- **`disco`, the colour engine's own egg: the eight rainbow colours step one position every second**, so every hued element moves to the next colour together while nothing else changes. It animates nothing - no keyframes, no new classes, no compositing layer. It steps the rotation offset rainbow already carried. `applyDisco()`, `discoTap()` and the three constants are in `reference/appearance.ts`.
- **The gesture: turn Rainbow Mode on five times within three seconds of each other.** Only turn-ons count, which halves the clicks and leaves the gesture ending with rainbow ON - the one state where a walking palette is visible at all. A reward that arrives invisible is a bug report waiting to happen.

## 🎨 Design

- **An ancestor's entrance may translate, never scale or rotate, whenever anything inside it animates.** A translation on an ancestor can be composited independently of its subtree, so the parent's layer moves and the children's stay where they are. A scale or a rotation cannot: the engine has to resample everything underneath through the parent's own matrix, which leaves every animating descendant holding a layer inside a parent being resampled around it. The page keyframe is the case that proves it, and the same rule governs any wrapper an app animates over a list, a card grid or a live indicator.
- **Fixing a bug by making it the non-default is mitigation, not a fix, because a changed default never reaches a stored choice.** Moving the motion default from `wild` to `subtle` was right on its own terms, since the top of the range had stopped being polish, and it stays. It was not a repair: the person who reported the flash met it again the moment they updated, and so did anybody who picks the top level on purpose.
- **A behaviour-changing easter egg may outrank a preference that protects people from things they did not choose.** Reverses what the storm's own entry said. The three levels a picker offers keep obeying `prefers-reduced-motion` unconditionally, because nobody who set it went looking for them. Five taps on an option already chosen is not a value anybody inherited.
- **Where that exemption lives is the whole design.** In the `reduce` block, which swaps in gentler substitutes rather than switching motion off - those substitutes are what make the storm a storm. Not in the `no-preference` block, which holds the press and the spinner.
- **Exempting is half of it; restoring is the half that gets forgotten.** The full rule sits in the block the media query replaced, so an exemption alone leaves the element quieter than the substitute it removed - and where its resting state is invisible, gone entirely with nothing in its place.
- **Both eggs stop at anything continuous.** Wanting more movement is not wanting something that never stops.
- **A gesture needs a time window when its component motion is ordinary.** Tapping a chosen option is not something anybody does by accident; toggling a mode on and off is how you compare two looks.
- **Distance, duration and curve are the whole set, and three dials are enough to tell the levels apart.** 18px against subtle's 6px, 420ms against 140ms, a spring that overshoots against a plain ease, with `storm` at 34px over 760ms. None of the three asks the compositor to resample anything.
- **A per-second writer is what tests whether an app's hue coverage is real.** A hue arrives as an inline style computed during render, so an element only recolours when its component renders again. Subscribe once above the routes. A setting only ever changed on one screen hides every missing subscription until something changes it from elsewhere.
- **A settings card CONFIGURES; the shell OPERATES.** Rule 22. A card that sets something up does not also carry the buttons that act on the live session - on a form with unsaved fields, those are the two controls that throw the form away, and one of them duplicated what the shell already offered.
- **Removing an operation from a card must not remove the CAPABILITY.** The test before deleting such a button is "where does this live once it is gone" - another surface, or the action that implies it. Signing every other session out moved into changing the password, which is what somebody changing it out of suspicion assumed was happening.
- **The control that starts an enrolment is named for the act, and every such control is named the same.** *Enable* on one card and *Add passkey* on the next made a reader work out whether the different wording meant a different thing. It does not. **It must carry a glyph**, because the glyph is then what tells two same-worded buttons apart, and the word is a per-language LOOKUP of what the app already says elsewhere, never a fresh translation.

## 🐛 Fixed

- **The page entrance scaled the whole route wrapper while its own contents animated.** `glim-page-in` ran `translateY()` and `scale()` together on the element the cards and rows animate inside, so each of those was resampled through the wrapper's matrix on every page change. Two engines gave two symptoms from that one cause: on Firefox/macOS the hued badges came out of uninitialised layer memory as a flat green (`#38FF38`), reported as a flash; on Chromium the colours were right and the double resampling showed as the page trembling before it settled. The keyframe is a `translateY` alone now.
- **`storm` loses the dial too, and it is the level that could least afford it.** The storm is exempt from the reduced-motion substitutes, which makes it the only level that still animates for somebody whose operating system asked for less motion - so it is the last place in the language that should be resampling a whole page. It keeps its 34px over 760ms on the furthest-overshooting curve, which is what the level was ever about.
- **The motion mechanism bullet named two tokens that have never existed.** `--motion-toast-slide-scale` and `--motion-shake-scale` were listed as the distance and amplitude tokens an intensity redefines; the real ones are `--motion-page-travel`, `--motion-curve` and `--glim-toast-slide` beside the five durations. A reader following that list finds nothing to tune.
- **The README's engine table gave the motion default as `wild`** after it had moved to `subtle`, so the one place an adopting app reads before copying anything disagreed with `DEFAULT_MOTION` and with the design language's own entry.
- **`GLIMSTONE_VERSION` had said `1.16.0` since before 2.0.0.** The number ships beside the reference files precisely so it cannot drift from them, and it drifted anyway: it names no version that was ever cut, so an About card reading it links to a release page that does not exist, which is the exact 404 the file was added to prevent. A release that changes anything in `reference/` bumps it.
